title: My mother is Korean and in her 60s. She's suffering from depression because she thinks she was a bad mother. She enjoys processing her emotions watching films and I was wondering if you had any recommendations for me?

commenti.body:
"Everything, Everywhere, All at Once" deals with this kind of familiar issue quite beautifully.   
Has she seen it?   
Fantastical movie about family and love and forgiveness of both oneself and others.

There is a YouTube channel called [Korean Film Classics](https://youtube.com/@koreanfilm?si=XvI7GlyFM6YTJq0q) that regularly posts old Korean films they’ve digitized. Hopefully there are some she might enjoy but I recommend 길소뜸 (Gilsoddeum) about a mother searching for her son.

'Mon Oncle', 1958 by Jacques Tati always cheers me up (I'm about the same age as your mom). I have chronic depression, and part of it is the rapid change from my youth to now, so I enjoy films from 'back in the day'. The entire premise of 'Mon Oncle' is the contrast between pre and post war France. It's subtitled, but is nearly devoid of dialog. It's now a film I watch almost every Christmas with my daughter when she returns.

Films can also point out how incredibly lucky I am - I haven't quite finished 'A Matter Of Life And Death' (1946) (Powell & Pressburger), but it's a cathartic three-handkerchief masterpiece.

I've discovered that being on the spectrum, watching films allows me to experience and interpret emotions in a measured way - I can watch the film again and again to understand the emotions expressed. If you can, watch them with her as well.

I'd also suggest whatever films she may have liked in her youth. Best of luck with her. I've been grateful for a low dose of sertraline for the past 20 years. They're not happy pills, but they provide a 'floor' so I never 'fall' too far!

The Namesake. A beautiful movie about the challenges of raising children in a different culture, imperfect relationships, and the sacrifices parents make for their children.

The screenplay was adapted from the book by Jhumpa Lahiri and directed by Mira Nair (who I first knew from Monsoon Wedding). There's a post-Harold and Kumar moody boy Kal Penn, and a stellar performance by Irrfan Khan. 

I showed this movie to my family, and it sparked a heart to heart between my cousin and my uncle. They had been having some issues, and this movie was the starting point for developing empathy for one another.
Wow, thanks for sharing that link! What a treasure trove.

Let her know you're happy. And that she had a huge part to play in that.


Let her know that her guilt is unnecessary and unfounded and that it bums you out a little bit and the next time those thoughts intrude, to remember this conversation and try to not focus on these thoughts. For you. 


Most of the movies that sorta fit are more father/son type stories like Road to Perdition. Just saw someone go with Everything, Everywhere, All at Once and I was thinking the same thing

I would highly suggest watching "Dark Water" (2001). This movie shows the struggles and flaws of a mother trying to take care of her daughter on her own but it is also a celebration and advocacy to mothers who do the most they can to watch over us even in times of mental and economic unwellness

I mean if you want her to go crazy with Korean slow-burn dramas that are pretty difficult but meaningful I would basically recommend everything Lee Chang Dong has put out; primarily Secret Sunshine and Poetry. They might be too dour and depressing, but idk I think they both do a really good job of demonstrating how to find joy/fulfillment when surrounded by depressing circumstances (especially Secret Sunshine, Poetry is a little bit more bleak). Also both are about mothers reflecting on their role of what being a mother really means. Mother by Bong Joon-ho might be good too and kinda fits in here, but its a little different and more crime adjacent. 

However I think for all 3 of these you should watch them first by yourself and screen them for your mom since only you would know if they would be meaningfully relevant or helpful to her situation. I remember absent mindedly showing Hereditary to a friend who had mom/family issues growing up and idk if that viewing experience was really a positive experience for him.

Petite Maman (2021)

The Farewell (2019)

The Joy Luck Club (1993)

I've Loved You So Long (2008)

The Lost Daughter (2011)

Volver (2006)

Divine Secrets of the YaYa Sisterhood (2002)

Terms of Endearment (1983)

Everything Everywhere All at Once (2022)

Postcards From the Edge (1990)



I don't know if any of these will be what you are looking for but they are what came to mind for me reading your post.

Hello, I’m sorry to hear about your mother’s depression. I too suffer from depression and I love to watch film help my mental health. Maybe ask her what her favorite movie(s) is and watch it with her. 

As far as recommendations go…
If your mom is willing to watch a “Chinese” movie (made by Americans about Chinese culture) I would suggest “Everything Everywhere All At Once” or “The Farewell”. Both movies deal with family and expectations. They are also both feel good movies. 

If she likes romance I would suggest maybe “eternal sunshine of the spotless mind” “Amelie” or maybe “stranger than fiction” 

Maybe a movie like “Hunt for the Wilderpeople” which is funny and about finding family could help. 

Hope this is helpful. Sorry that I don’t know many Korean films that fit your needs. 

Let me know if you need anymore recommendations or want stuff more specific.
Lee Chang Dong is my favorite director of all time--glad to see him recommended here.

Postcards from the Edge and Volver would be great for this subject. Also both movies I consider quite cozy.


The Farewell made me cry like a baby, as my grandmother has JUST passed. Then I followed it up with Marcel the Shell with Shoes On which did the same thing.
Oh Petite Maman is such a good call, what a beautiful and strange film.
Oh man. Thank you. I'll take a look at these.

First, it is great that you are looking after your mother's mental health, it is a noble thing to do and you should recognize that trading "roles" with your parent can be a big deal, and might impact you negatively, so you should make sure to get support for your mental health. But it can also be very rewarding, and it is a way to repay the love and attention she has given you. 

I would suggest the movies of Hirokazu Koreeda, many deal with parental/filial relationships such as Still Walking; Like Father, Like Son; Shoplifters; After the Storm; and Broker. As someone else suggested, I would recommend watching 1-3 of them to see if you think it would be a good fit for your mother given the different themes and nuances.

I’ve found that people who have spent most of their lives in eastern culture don’t relate well to that film I’ve found that people who have spent most of their lives in eastern culture don’t relate well to that film I’ve found that people who have spent most of their lives in eastern culture don’t relate well to that film
Thank you. I appreciate you comment dearly.
I'll take a look at this. Thank you.
I try my best to be fair to her because she's not in a condition to be fair to herself. Thanks for the recommendations I appreciate you

Minari is a beautiful and nuanced family drama that would likely resonate with you. The film follows a Korean-American family's move to rural Arkansas in the 1980s. It’s a character study with a subtle storytelling; exploring themes of resilience, cultural identity, and family dynamics.

I'd recommend Yiyi! it doesn't necessarily focus too much on a mother-daughter relationship, but the entire movie is about the dynamics and different "coming of age" issues experienced across the generations of a Taiwanese family. it's very bittersweet but ultimately optimistic and was a cathartic watch for me

Not technically a movie, but I think she will really enjoy watching Pachinko. it revolves around the Korean occupation and the perseverance of Korean identity from then till modern times. Very emotional, nuanced, and explores the family dynamic amongst Korean families. It’s extremely well done.

Maybe some classic Korean films?

https://www.filmlinc.org/series/korean-cinemas-golden-decade-the-1960s/#films

The Lincoln Center had a film festival last year about Korea's Golden Decade. There might be something in there for your mom...

I think Tokyo Story is a perfect movie about the infinite highs and lows relationships face, especially those between parents and children. It is beyond poignant, so I am not sure if that is the move. Yi Yi also deals with family, but just also all life. It is very sad but also possibly hopeful. Someone recommended Still Walking by Kore-eda, which definitely fits the themes of family very well. I think After Life (same director) falls less into the appropriate category but has a plethora of emotions that one can takeaway from the movie.

"Goodbye Lenin" (Germany 2003) is a beautiful film about a son lying to protect his mother and then finding out she did something similar for him and his sister to keep them safe. 


[Wikipedia](https://ko.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/%EA%B5%BF%EB%B0%94%EC%9D%B4_%EB%A0%88%EB%8B%8C) says that a Korean dub exists.

> Minari

I has said Minari as well, but looks like my comment didn't meet the length requirement.  I highly recommend this movie to anyone that hasn't seen it.

Unfortunately I feel it’s hard to recommend a lot of Korean films because they tend to be…well, they’re a lot. However, I think Mother (2009) might hit in just the right places.

Also, The Farewell, Alice Doesn’t Live Here Anymore, Mildred Pierce, Everything Everywhere All At Once. Depends on what kinds of feelings she’s wishing to indulge or perhaps exorcise, but I think there’s a decent mix of perspectives from both mother/parent and child in those.
Secret Sunshine is a *rough* watch, it’s up there with Peppermint Candy and Come and See as the most despairing films I’ve ever seen.

Yeah I totally agree it's rough, it's why I think OP should screen the films and make sure they're appropriate for his mom's context (I don't want her depression to get worse) but I do think Song Kang-Ho's character adds a lightness to Secret Sunshine the other two movies don't really have.
